summary:
We built TerraSpace Explorer because we wanted a simple answer to a hard question: where on Earth can we practise for the Moon and Mars?

It’s a website with an interactive world map of 24 candidate sites. Each one is colour-coded by whether it looks more like the Moon, more like Mars, a bit of both, or is a newly discovered place that needs more study. You can filter by terrain, such as deserts, volcanic regions, impact craters, caves and polar areas. Click any site and you get its elevation, slope, temperature range, rainfall, and how closely it matches the Moon and Mars. The Atacama Desert in Chile, for example, scores 56.2% for the Moon and 74.2% for Mars. You can also adjust the scoring weights and compare sites side by side.

Behind it all is NASA data, including NASA POWER, ASTER GDEM, the Planetary Data System, Moon and Mars Trek and USGS Landsat.

This matters because testing rovers, habitats and astronaut routines on Earth is far cheaper and safer than testing them in space. We were also careful to be honest about the limits. A high score marks terrain worth studying, not proof that a place is equivalent, and the site shows which results are field-measured and which come from a catalog baseline.
details:
What it does and how it works:

TerraSpace Explorer is an interactive website that helps people find places on Earth that resemble the Moon and Mars. The centrepiece is a world map of 24 candidate sites, colour-coded as Moon primary analog, Mars primary analog, dual Moon and Mars fit, or newly discovered and needing study. You can search or filter by terrain (polar, desert, volcanic, impact crater, caves and tubes, high-altitude) and click any site to open its profile. The profile shows elevation, slope, temperature range, precipitation, a geological description, data sources and Moon and Mars similarity scores. Other pages cover an overview dashboard, Moon and Mars comparisons, similarity analysis with adjustable scoring weights, a resource explorer and a NASA data sources page. When a site is inspected, the site fetches live NASA POWER, ASTER GDEM and USGS Landsat measurements.

Benefits and intended impact:

Researchers, students and mission planners can compare many sites in one place instead of searching scattered sources. Analog sites let teams test rovers, habitats, instruments and astronaut procedures on Earth, which is cheaper and safer than testing in space. We hope the platform supports early-stage site selection for future Moon bases and Mars missions, as well as training and education.

Tools and technology:

We built the interface with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with responsive navigation. The map uses Leaflet with OpenStreetMap and CARTO base tiles, and the site is hosted on Netlify. Data comes from NASA POWER, Earthdata (ASTER GDEM), the Planetary Data System, Moon and Mars Trek, GIBS, EONET, NASA Open APIs and USGS Landsat. No special hardware was needed.

What makes it creative:

Instead of a static list of analog sites, we built a scoring tool. Users can tune the weights, see Moon and Mars fit side by side, and spot newly discovered regions that are under-explored.

What we considered:

Scientific honesty was our main concern. The site states that high similarity marks candidate terrain for study, not validated equivalence. It also separates 8 field-measured sites from catalog-baseline entries, so users can judge how reliable each result is. We also made it easy to use on different screen sizes.
